title: Maximum Palindromes After Operations
statement:
You are given an array `words` of lowercase strings. As many times as you like (possibly never), you may pick any two character positions anywhere in `words`, in the same string or in two different strings, and exchange the characters stored there. The strings keep their lengths.

Return the largest number of strings in `words` that can all be palindromes at the same time after your swaps.
constraints: words[i] contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Swaps can carry any character to any position, so the original arrangement does not matter: only the pool of letters and the length of each string do. A palindrome of length `L` is `L / 2` (rounded down) pairs of equal letters mirrored around the centre, plus one free middle letter when `L` is odd. Middle letters never run short, because whatever letters are not used in pairs fill the remaining slots. So the only scarce resource is the number of equal-letter pairs in the pool, and to make the most palindromes we should spend pairs on the cheapest (shortest) strings first. Trying every subset would also work, but only for a handful of strings.

## Approach

1. Count every letter across all of `words` into `count`.
2. Add `floor(c / 2)` for every letter count `c` to get `pairs`, the total number of matched pairs.
3. Sort the string lengths in increasing order.
4. For each `length`, it needs `need = floor(length / 2)` pairs. If there are not enough left, stop; otherwise spend them and count one more palindrome in `made`.
5. Return `made`.

## Example 1, step by step

`words = ["abbb", "ba", "aa"]` has four `a` and four `b`, so `pairs = 2 + 2 = 4`. The sorted lengths are `[2, 2, 4]`.

- Length 2 needs 1 pair: `pairs = 3`, `made = 1`.
- Length 2 needs 1 pair: `pairs = 2`, `made = 2`.
- Length 4 needs 2 pairs: `pairs = 0`, `made = 3`.

The answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(T + n log n): one pass over all `T` characters, then sorting the `n` lengths.
- Space: O(n) for the sorted lengths, plus 26 counters.

## Pitfalls

- Pairs are pooled across all strings; counting them per string misses the point of the swaps.
- Odd-length strings need the same number of pairs as the even length below them; their middle letter is free.
- Sort by length ascending: a long string can cost as many pairs as several short ones.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | how many times each letter appears across `words` |
| `pairs` | matched pairs still available |
| `lengths` | string lengths, sorted ascending |
| `need` | pairs the current string requires |
| `made` | palindromes formed so far |
